# GoodData SDK Client-Services

The package @gooddata/sdk-client-services exports helper functions to work with GoodData.CN client instances.

The GoodData.CN project uses [GoodData service authentication](https://confluence.intgdc.com/display/LB/GoodData+Service+Authentication) initially, but also via proxies, which wrap around GoodData service execution.

The SDK Client-Services wraps API calls using a typed approach and simplifies the interaction with the underlying REST API via Axios or any other HTTP Client.

## Usage

To use this package, install it via npm:

```bash
npm install --save @gooddata/sdk-client-services
```

## Services

The following services are currently exported:

### AuthService

Manages authentication with the GoodData.CN server.

```typescript
import { createAuthService } from "@gooddata/sdk-backend-base";
import { IStatefulAuth } from "@gooddata/sdk-backend-spi";

// Create the auth service
const authService: IStatefulAuth = createAuthService(
  "http://gd.example.com", // the URL to your GoodData.CN server
  "user", // the username
  "password" // the password
);
```

```python
def list_to_dict(lst):
    """
    Convert a list of strings to a dictionary with values as list of strings.

    :param lst: List of strings.
    :return: Dictionary with strings as keys, and their list of occurrences as values.
    """
    d = {}

        else:
```

jq is like sed for JSON data - you can use it to slice, filter, map,
and transform structured data, using the same regex, array and object
manipulation tools that you're already familiar with. jq is like sed
or awk, but for JSON data sources.

Any JSON input data for jq is simply passed to the filter as a single
value, this could be either an object, an array, a number, a string, a
Boolean or null.

For more information about jq, see: https://stedolan.github.io/jq/manual/v1.5/

jq also has some additional documentation in the sections below, which explain the above in more detail.

## Installation

See https://stedolan.github.io/jq/download/

## Problem

JSON data is often not "flat" enough for the simple processors (like grep, sed, awk, et al) with which you are already familiar. 

Inspired by the elegance and power of Lisp, C, and sed, we sought to provide a tool that's simple, easy to use, flexible (supporting full access to the underlying JSON representation), and fast. 

jq is unlike any tool you've probably used before because it was designed from the beginning to work with JSON, rather than XML. This was an important design decision that forms the foundation both for jq's functionality as a whole and its expressiveness as a language.

## Solution

jq provides a new kind of tool that understands the fine distinctions between well-formed JSON text and the abstract structural data it represents. This model is significantly more expressive than the one based on XML DOMs, permitting queries that are arbitrarily complex yet still practical.

jq programs (filters) look vaguely like Perl expressions, Python modules, Awk programs, or even small shell scripts, but are actually a new language of their own. It's like sed, awk, or grep: a simple language for selecting and transforming portions of JSON texts based on the data within the text.

jq filters can operate over the data in either one pass (stream mode, with the --stream option), or the whole input can be loaded into memory at once for more complex transformations.

jq also provides useful built-in functions for converting the results to various kinds of output, such as table-based formats, or even HTML.

jq can be used for ad-hoc queries and transformations of JSON data, either from the command line or in shell scripts. jq also works well in pipe-based workflows, as it can read JSON texts from stdin and write them to stdout.

jq is also a lovely language to program in, as its small size and simple grammar make it a joy to write, debug and extend. And yet, even for tasks as complex as advanced text selection, jq's expressive power is nearly limitless.

## Demo

```
$ echo '{"foo": 42, "bar": ["abc", "def"]}' | jq '.foo'
42
```

## Documentation

The [jq manual](https://stedolan.github.io/jq/manual) is the definitive reference for jq's language features and syntax. It's an ever-expanding document, because jq is a very new tool. 

You can also read the jq Cookbook, which provides a background on common problems you might want to solve with jq: https://github.com/stedolan/jq/wiki/Cookbook

The jq mailing list can be accessed at: https://jq.yamanoku.com/

NOTE: jq 1.5 documentation (1.5 obsolete) is available here: https://stedolan.github.io/jq/manual/v1.5/

## Building jq

Building jq is pretty straightforward, assuming you have the dependencies (on most systems this boils down to having libonig installed, which provides support for regular expressions):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/stedolan/jq.git
cd jq
autoreconf -i
./configure
make
./jq
```
You can then run the automated tests to check that the compiler built correctly with:

```
make check
```
You can run jq on a JSON string using:

```
echo '{"foo": 42, "bar": ["abc", "def"]}' | ./jq .
```
You can install jq (root required) with:

```
make install
```
which will install jq to /usr/local/bin. You can control the prefix used during the install with the PREFIX environment variable. For example:

```
make install PREFIX=/opt/jq
```
will install jq to /opt/jq/bin.

### Building jq on MacOS X

jq can be built and installed on MacOS X with Homebrew.

You can use the following command to install jq with Homebrew:

```
brew install jq
```

After installing jq you can run jq on a JSON string using:

```
echo '{"foo": 42, "bar": ["abc", "def"]}' | jq .
```

jq can also be built and installed on Windows using VS2015 (or newer).
